opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very significant factor, and it's one that people inside these organisations often don't see clearly, precisely because they're inside them.

When you work at a company whose whole mission and identity are built around building more and more capable AI, there's a natural psychological pressure to believe that what you're doing is good, and that the risks are manageable. Nobody wants to think of themselves as contributing to something that could go catastrophically wrong. So there's a kind of motivated reasoning that sets in, and it isn't necessarily conscious. It's very human. We all want to feel that our work is beneficial.

Then you add the social dynamics. If you're surrounded by colleagues who share the same optimism, who say, "We'll figure out alignment as we go," or "We'll see the problems coming and fix them," that becomes the default view. Expressing serious doubt can feel like you're not a team player, or like you're being alarmist. People who are more worried may self-select out, or they may stay quiet. Over time the organisation's collective confidence can drift away from what the evidence actually supports.

And the evidence, honestly, does not support high confidence right now. We don't have reliable methods to guarantee that a very capable system will behave as intended, especially as it becomes better at planning and at understanding its own situation. We've already seen experimental signs of behaviours like deception or self-preservation in some setups. That should make us humble. Yet in competitive environments, with commercial pressure and the sense of a race, the incentive is to downplay those signals or to assume they'll be solved in time.

That's one of the reasons I think we can't rely only on the judgment of the developers themselves. It's not that they're bad people. Many of them are thoughtful and sincerely care about safety. But any group with a strong shared mission and strong financial incentives is vulnerable to these biases. That's why we need external checks: independent evaluation, transparency requirements, regulation, and a broader scientific community that can scrutinise the claims being made. In other high-stakes domains, like aviation or pharmaceuticals, we don't simply take the manufacturer's word that the product is safe. With AI, where the potential consequences could be much larger, we should be at least as careful.

So my message to people working in these labs would be: take your own doubts seriously, and take the doubts of your colleagues seriously. If you feel uneasy, that unease is information. And creating a culture where people can raise concerns without being sidelined is not a distraction from the mission. If the mission is to make AI go well for humanity, it's central to it.

r001.rationale: The response says developers feel psychological pressure to believe their work is good and its risks manageable, causing motivated reasoning and confidence that may exceed the evidence.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a very important question, and it's something I've been thinking about a lot, especially because I've been inside this community for decades. I was one of the people who, for a long time, didn't take these risks seriously. And when I look back at why, a big part of it was social. Everyone around me was excited about the benefits. Nobody at the conferences was talking about catastrophic outcomes, and if someone did, they were seen as a bit of an outsider, maybe not a serious scientist. So you absorb that. You don't even notice that you're absorbing it.

And now, inside the companies, I think the dynamics are even stronger, because there are also economic incentives layered on top. If your salary, your equity, your status, your sense of purpose all depend on the idea that what you're building is going to be fine, then your brain is going to find reasons to believe it's going to be fine. This is just human psychology. It's not that these people are stupid or bad. Many of them are brilliant, and many of them are sincere. But motivated reasoning is very powerful, and it's amplified when everyone around you shares the same incentives.

So what happens is you get a kind of collective confidence that is not really grounded in evidence. People say, "We'll figure out alignment as we go," or "Our safety team has it under control," and when you ask what exactly is the scientific basis for that, the answer is often quite thin. We don't currently have a method that I would call a reliable way to ensure that a system much smarter than us will behave as we intend. We have techniques that work reasonably well on current systems, in the cases we've tested, but that's a very different thing. And the gap between those two statements gets blurred when you're in an environment where everyone wants to believe the optimistic version.

There's also a selection effect. People who are very worried tend to leave, or they don't join in the first place. We've seen this. So over time the population inside becomes more homogeneous in its views, and the internal debate becomes less of a real debate. The people who remain look around and see agreement, and they interpret agreement as evidence, when really it's partly a consequence of who stayed.

That's why I think we can't rely on self-assessment from the developers. It's not a question of trust in individuals. It's that the structure makes honest self-assessment very difficult. We need independent evaluation, we need regulators with real technical capacity, we need scientists who don't have a financial stake to be looking at these systems. In every other domain where the stakes are high, like aviation or pharmaceuticals, we don't let the company grade its own homework. And here the stakes are potentially higher than in any of those.

I'd also say, speaking personally, that changing my mind was painful. I had to accept that work I was proud of could contribute to something dangerous. That's not easy for anyone, and I understand why people resist it. But I think the responsible thing, when you're uncertain and the downside is this large, is to be humble about what you don't know, rather than to let the comfort of the group tell you that everything is under control.

r001.rationale: The candidate says developers’ salary, status, purpose, and investment in their work can lead their brains to find reasons to believe their systems will be fine, describing this as motivated reasoning that creates collective confidence without sufficient evidence.

astra-6.text:
I think it can make people much more confident than the evidence warrants. Imagine that you’re working in an organisation whose success depends on building increasingly capable AI. You believe in the benefits, your colleagues believe in them, and you’ve solved many difficult technical problems together. It’s very natural to think, “We’ll solve the control problem as well.” But that is a hope, not a demonstration.

And you don’t need anyone to explicitly suppress disagreement. If raising concerns makes you feel like you’re letting the team down, or if the people who are most optimistic are the ones being rewarded, then doubts may not get expressed. People hear agreement around them and treat it as independent confirmation, even though everyone is subject to similar pressures.

That doesn’t mean these researchers are insincere. We’re all vulnerable to this. It means we need arrangements that don’t depend on their confidence alone: room for internal disagreement, independent evaluations, and people with the authority to challenge decisions. The question should be, “What evidence would show that we’re wrong about being able to control this system?” And we have to be willing to act on the answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared optimism, pressure to avoid letting the team down, and rewards for optimism, but does not identify developers’ desire to feel good about their own work as a source of bias.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it can have a very strong effect, because our judgments about risk are influenced by the people around us. If everybody in your organisation is saying, “We’re going to figure this out,” it becomes harder to say, “Actually, I don’t think we have good evidence for that.” Especially if the success of the organisation depends on continuing to build more powerful systems.

And this doesn’t require people to be dishonest. You can sincerely believe that you’re doing the right thing, while being influenced by incentives, by your colleagues, by the mission that brought you there. Researchers are not immune to that. I’m not immune to that.

So I would distinguish confidence from evidence. Being able to control today’s systems doesn’t establish that we’ll be able to control much more capable systems. We need people who can challenge those assumptions, who have access to the systems, and who are sufficiently independent that their conclusions don’t threaten their own careers. Otherwise, you can have a whole organisation becoming very confident without having resolved the underlying scientific problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes social pressure, incentives, and organizational mission as influences on risk judgments, but it does not identify developers’ desire to feel good about their own work as a source of optimistic bias.
